utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. As the members of the Prosecution are somewhat different today, could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and to everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Vassily Poryvaev, Miguel Longone, and our case manager Skye Winner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. The members of Defence counsel have not changed. It's not necessary to have the appearances. I'd like to greet everyone present in the courtroom; the accused, members of the Prosecution, and the Defence counsel and everyone else in the courtroom. We'll be continuing with our work today, and we'll be calling a new witness. Prior to calling the new witness, we would have two oral decisions that we would like to render that concern questions put to us last week. On standby we had the issue of two video sequences, two video clips. A request was made to have them admitted on the 16th of May, 2006. This was a Prosecution request. P 01015 is the number that the video was marked with for identification. The second video clip was entitled "Greater Croatia," the number was P 07437, marked for identification. Given the explanations provided to us by Belinda Giles, the witness Belinda Giles, and given what was said in the course of the hearing, we believe that it is necessary to admit these two video clips as exhibits. Mr. Registrar, could we have the numbers for these exhibits, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. These two exhibits will be admitted into evidence under the following numbers: [In English] The first video is admitted under the reference P 01015. The second video is admitted under the reference P 07437. I also note for the record that both videos are admitted with their respective transcripts. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Now for the send oral decision. The accused Coric had a motion that concerned the expert Donia's report. On the 15th of May, 2006, the accused Coric stated that he was opposed to having the expert witness's report admitted as evidence. This concerned Donia, the Donia report. The accused Coric also said that if his motion was rejected, he would request that his arguments be taken into consideration when determining the probative value of the report. The Chamber wants to remind you that on the 15th of May, 2006, they decided on the admissibility of Donia's report, and this report was given the number P 09356. As a result, the motion of the accused Coric has been rejected. As far as the second part of the request is concerned, the Chamber would like to remind you that the arguments presented in the motion will naturally be taken into consideration at the time that the Chamber decides on the probative value of the report in question. Those are the two oral decisions I wanted to render today. Without wasting any more time, we will now call the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Usher, would please call the witness into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Last week I contacted the Registry with regard to appointing counsel. They said that the documents had been sent to the Chamber. Time is passing by and I would like a member of the team to be admitted to the case as soon as possible. Therefore I would be grateful if you could provide me with some information as to when this matter could be dealt with. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Coric, for that. We the Judges will discuss it and we will then inform you of your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying into your own language. If so, please say that you can hear and understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have been called here as a witness for the Prosecution. Before you read out the solemn declaration, could you please tell me what your first and last names are and also your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Fahrudin Rizvanbegovic. I was born on the 4th of February, 1945, in the town of Stolac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me what your current profession is, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now a university professor in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, have you already testified before an international court or before a national court with regard to the events that took place in your country in 1993 and 1994? Is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please could you read out the solemn declaration now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, before I give the floor to the Prosecution who will conduct your examination-in-chief -- who will conduct their examination-in-chief, I'd like to provide you with some information regarding the procedure we'll be following. First of all, you will have to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution. They are to your right and you certainly met them when you were proofed for the hearing. Once this phase has been completed, Defence counsel, who are to your left, will conduct the cross-examination. And you will notice that the questions put to you in the course of the cross-examination are quite different from the type of questions put to you by the Prosecution. Remain calm. Do your best to answer the questions in a clear way. If you encounter any difficulties, do inform us of the fact. The four Judges sitting before you may at any point in time, if they deem it necessary, put questions to you, questions that you are here to answer. But as a rule; we prefer to wait for both parties to finish putting their questions to you before we intervene. As you have just taken the solemn declaration, this means that you should avoid giving false testimony, which is a violation that is punishable by this Tribunal. These are the rough guidelines I wanted to provide you with. In addition, I'd like to point out that every one and a half hours we have a short 20-minute break, and then we continue for an hour and a half and have another 20-minute break. If you feel uneasy or if you have any difficulties of any kind in the course of the hearing, inform me of the fact and we can have a break. Having said that, I will now give the floor to the Prosecution for their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. First I must introduce myself again. To the Trial Chamber first of all, my name is Vassily Poryvaev. It's not my first trial here and always the Trial Chamber, the Judge had problems with my full name although it's not very difficult. It's pronounced Poryvaev, and if you have some doubt or forget it, I will not feel offended if you call me Mr. Prosecutor. Having said that, I'm not pretending to be the next after Carla Del Ponte, her deputy, my senior trial attorneys and so on, it's just a practical matter. Mr. Rizvanbegovic, you just told the Trial Chamber that your current occupation is professor of Sarajevo University. Let's go back a little bit to your background, and I will lead a couple of questions just to abbreviate this part of the examination-in-chief. From 1964 to 1968, you studied in Zagreb in the faculty of philosophy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Then you completed your master degree and post-doctorate in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: In Zagreb, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Then for some period of time, for three years, you were working as professor in the high school and high school for juvenile criminals; correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, were you ever you involved in any social activities apart from your permanent job as a professor?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As a student, and later on as a professor, I was involved in various social activities, but on the whole I was involved in cultural activities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of Council of the Congress of Bosnian Intellectuals?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a permanent member of the Congress of Bosnian Intellectuals. I'm a member of the Congress today as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What about your family status? Are you married, have children?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm married. I have two children. My children are professors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What is your place of residence now?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I live in Sarajevo. I live in Sarajevo and in Stolac. I spend half the week in Sarajevo and the other half in Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, did you belong to any political party before the collapse of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: There was only one party at the time, and I was a member of that party for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you join any political party shortly after the collapse of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: When I left that party, which I did voluntarily a few years before the war -- well, after I had left that party I didn't join any other parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, since you were born in Stolac and lived many years there, I suggest you should know about the demographic situation in Stolac municipality. Let's begin with 1991. I mean, the last official census before the war. I -- I --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: That was the last census. That was the last census before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: After that date, there were no other censuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Could you tell me what was the ethnic composition of the population of the Stolac municipality in 1991?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can answer that question precisely, but out of 18.000-odd inhabitants, I would say that 44 per cent of them were Bosniaks, 33 per cent were -- per cent were Croats, 21 per cent were Serbs, and the others were people who were not members of any of those three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I suggest, Witness, you are giving some approximate figures to the Trial Chamber. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The figures are approximate. I didn't realise that this is something I should have known, but as an intellectual, yes, I have some knowledge of the approximate numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the registrar to help me and show the witness Exhibit P 08559.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, I see that I don't have a copy of the document. I apologise. It was the registrar's fault for not having provided me with a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: It's page 3, line 25. Year 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be enlarged, the part that relates to Stolac? That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you agree that the data that we have here on the whole corresponds to your testimony about the ethnic structure of the population in 1991?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think this is from the Statistical Institute, that this information comes from the Statistical Institute, and these figures are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When did the first municipal elections take place in Stolac municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When did the first municipal elections take place in the municipality Stolac?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It's a well-known fact that this was in the 1990s. That's when the elections were held. Elections were held throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was also the case in Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Were those elections held in a multi-party system?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Those were the first multi-party elections held in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And which party --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Which party won the elections?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian Democratic Union received the largest number of votes, the second party was the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, and the third party was the SDS, as far as I can remember. Those were the three nationalist parties. And after those three parties, the SDP received the largest number of votes; Social Democrat Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what was the role of the leading party, which was HDZ, in the setting up of civilian authorities in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The HDZ provided the president of the municipality, whereas the SDA appointed the president of the Executive Committee. The SDS provided the chief economy and for certain other activities. I think that that is how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who was elected the president of municipality?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the municipality was Zeljko Raguz.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who was elected the president of government, of the government, the executive body?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The President of the Executive Board was Alija Rizvanbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: How long did he hold his position as chief of Executive Board? I mean Rizvanbegovic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Alija Rizvanbegovic was the president of the Executive Board until the 12th of June, 1992; until the time that the Croats who had fled from Stolac returned, on the 12th of July [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, we will come back to this issue a little bit later but now we will switch on to some other questions. It is a fact well known that by the decision of the 19th of November, 1991, Herceg-Bosna Community was created. When did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I learned about that decision very late. I learned about it in, once I had got out of the concentration camp. I knew that that community had been established, but I wasn't aware of the date. This is something that I found out in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But when did you observe that the structural power in Stolac municipality - or Mostar municipality, since you were working there - started changing?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this happened in Stolac on two occasions; first in April when the Serbian --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: -- army arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992. 1992. Most of the Croats fled. Only about 150 of them stayed on, those who were undesirable, so to speak, those who didn't agree with the HDZ. The president of the municipality, Zeljko Raguz, left with them too, so that the Executive Board took control of the town after the Croats had returned to Stolac. Zeljko Raguz was the president again, but for a very brief period of time. He was then rapidly replaced by Andjelko Markovic. So there were these changes. Alija Rizvanbegovic was expelled from Stolac. They threatened to arrest him for cooperating with the Serbs, and other conditions were established in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, were you familiar with Andjelko Markovic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know him well. I knew him by sight. He worked as a doctor in hospital for bone diseases, and my sister worked there, so I knew him from before the war. My sister is also a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what happened in the Stolac municipality that the Croats fled it in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian troops appeared. They passed through Stolac, so to speak. Some of the troops remained in Stolac. They continued in the direction of Capljina. They stopped at the entrance to Capljina. Stolac had been completely enclosed from that point in time onwards, and at that time the Croats set off in the direction of the Neretva, Pocitrn [phoen], and Capljina, and they would cross the Neretva. They would have to pass by Serbian tanks on the way. And naturally we weren't aware of that immediately, only after they had left. Not even my friends informed me of the fact, and I had a lot of Croatian friends there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So let's say that the local military formation did not put up any resistance to the Serbs' aggression.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: There practically was no local military formation of any kind. At least, I was unaware of its existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what was the power continued functioning in the Stolac municipality during the Serb occupation?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: During the Serb occupation, the Municipal Assembly continued working. It was mostly composed of Assemblymen who were members of the SDA, SDP, and the SDS. I think that they met only once or twice but not after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us, were there any attacks on the Serb forces against the local population of Stolac municipality?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when they came and passed through Stolac, there were no attacks. However, there was very intense fire from artillery or infantry weaponry, and naturally that caused a lot of fear among the population, especially since they could see that that wasn't the army acting in a regular way, if one could say so, but, rather, an army that wanted to intimidate civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Were there any mass destructions or damages caused to businesses, dwellings, cultural objects, religious sites?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period while this army was staying in town, not a single facility was destroyed in town itself. We were unable to leave Stolac, and I heard and later saw myself that in Dubrava the houses owned by various people were destroyed whereas in town itself not a single monument or facility was destroyed up until the 12th of April -- no, I apologise, 12th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When did the Serbs leave the area of Stolac?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 12th and the 13th of June, the Serbs withdrew from Stolac. There was some minor combat in Osanici, which is an old area above Stolac, above the town. In town itself, there was no significant combat. And at that point it was completely clear that there had been an agreement between the two sides who decided to draw a border in the area where the border between the nowadays Federation and Republika Srpska runs. I was in town, and I saw this in town. I don't know what was happening outside of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanbegovic, just -- we're talking about 12th and 13th of June. Which year??

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: 1992. All of this pertains to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what about the line of defence? Did the Serb forces try to recapture Stolac??

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: There were some fake attempts, pseudo-attempts in the course of 1992, but to my knowledge there were no real attempts to do that. They held the lines, the positions established at that time, and these positions remained there until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What units were the first to enter Stolac and, let's say, kick out the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The first units which entered Stolac were those of HOS. Behind them came the Croatian army from Metkovici, Ploce, and Split. And then there was the Dubrava-Stolac battalion of the Territorial Defence. The HVO was in the second echelon as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know what particular HVO units entered the town?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was the unit under the command of Nedjeljko Radovic [phoen]. This unit entered town together with other units. The commander of the Stolac segment was somebody with the last name of Pavlovic. I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to clarify the full name of the commander. Nedjeljko --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Was Pavlovic's unit subordinate to Nedjeljko Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the war it was subordinated to the unit under the command of Obradovic. I believe he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What other units were deployed in the area after the Serb defeat?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: As I have already mentioned, there was a unit from Metkovici, the 116th Unit under the command of Beneta. I had occasion to meet him once they arrived there, and this is how I know that he was the commander of the unit. Then there was the Stolac Unit, which had logistical ties to the 116th Unit. The logistical support, the supplies for this unit in Stolac arrived from Metkovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Metkovici Brigade, from where was that unit?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: This unit was from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the first Croatian town in the vicinity of Stolac. I went to that town almost on a weekly basis because we used to all live in one country. After that, I went with a friend of mine, Miroslav Palameta, to that unit. We were supposed to go there so he could see why the food hadn't arrived on time and the funds for salaries for soldiers. So this is how I know that this is what happened, because I went with him several times when he lodged in his protests.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What kind of protest did you lodge?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The protests were not lodged by me. Rather, by my colleague. He protested about the lunch not arriving on time, salaries not arriving on time. It was some kind of a verbal protest. He went there to inquire about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: How long did this unit stay in Stolac municipality?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how long it stayed there because I myself didn't visit the positions and various lines, and I didn't know which positions were held by which unit, but I think that it stayed there for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, you just told the Trial Chamber that all former authorities which left the town during the Serbs' occupation came back. Were they functioning after June 1992 in their former composition?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was only the military authorities that were functioning, those of the HVO. That was practically the only authority functioning in Stolac. This is why Zeljko Raguz left the office of the president, but I'm not sure exactly about the relations between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And in general, when the HVO Presidency was set up in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was established back while they were near Ploce in Gradac, in the Makarska area. I don't have detailed information about that, but I think that they were established there while they were in exile. We didn't know that such units existed until they arrived in Stolac. Stolac had Territorial Defence which was supposed to be a legitimate organisation. When the Croats arrived in Stolac, the residents had to put on their houses "TO" or "TO-HVO," and it was only then that we learned for the first time that there existed something called the HVO, those of us who were surrounded there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what coat of arms did they have?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It was a Croatian coat of arms. When they came to Stolac, all types of old signs and inscriptions were taken off. I saw with my own eyes Marijan Prce and some other people doing that, taking down the signs, and gradually they put up new signs with the various inscriptions of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And were all these signs of new power accepted by the population?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Other than Croats, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanbegovic, did you continue working at the Mostar university at that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was unable to leave Stolac during the Serb occupation. The first time I was able to go to Mostar was on the 25th of June, and I went to the university because I was deputy dean of the pedagogical department, the teacher training department. So I to my department, and I found in Mostar a military unit, which was quite a surprise for me. I looked for the dean. His name was Rudolf Kraljevic. He had been absent for quite a while. I asked that the documents and the records which were strewn in the corridor be gathered and put in order. I asked the soldiers to do that. That university or, rather, that department had records going back to -- going back 40 years, and I wanted that to be protected. These records pertain to various things, including alumni and so on. I had some problems with the commander and also somebody else threatening me, saying he would kill me and what was I doing there, interfering with their business? Following that, I went to the office of the president of the university to see what was to be done about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, let's wait a little bit. We'll come back to the issue of university a little bit later, but now could you get Mostar quite freely without any impediments?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, throughout that period until I was taken to the concentration camp, I and also other Bosniaks were unable to leave Stolac without a written permit. We would wait in lines for these permits to allow us to go to Mostar, to Capljina, to see our relatives in Dubrava or anywhere else. We had to wait for something that we at the time, recognising what was going on, referred to as "ausweiss". They were issuing permits on forms displaying signs of Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I think that's what it was called at the time. A special office was established to deal exclusively with these permits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did these rules --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. In addition to that, there were a large number of checkpoints where they checked for these papers to see whether we had them. One couldn't leave without them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who was running the checkpoints? Who was in command of checkpoints? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers. I think it was the military police. I wasn't paying attention to their insignia, though, but they were definitely the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did these rules of "ausweiss" apply only to the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think that it was in place only for Muslim residents and for the few remaining Serbs there. I'm not sure as to how many Croats took out those permits. I don't know anything about that. I'm not sure. I know for a fact that the Muslims had to have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And let's go back to the university issues. What was the main problem there at that time when you came there in June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The first session of the university council, whose member I was, was scheduled for the 26th of June, I believe, and it was convened in order to change the name of the university, to change the curriculum, to change the language of the instruction into exclusively Croatian language. This was proposed not by the president of the university or his deputy but, rather, by Bozo Zepic. I think he was a professor of Marxism back in the socialist system, and I think this is how he tried to gain more prominence for himself. The changes were aimed at amending the very essence, the very essential image of the university. Bozo Coric, the president of the university at the time, objected. Soon thereafter, he resigned, left the university, went to live in Zagreb where he lives to this day. I have very good relations with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And was this problem solved, I mean the problem of the university status, the language of instruction, and other issues?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we, the professors who were members of the council, were unable to accept something like that. I remember that I personally proposed that Mostar University not be called a Croatian university but, rather, university in Mostar or Mostar University. And I remember that I even joked about the word they were proposing for "university," "sveuciliste," saying that that was a word of a Serbian origin first used in Novi Sad. Unfortunately, they didn't accept my joke well. Some professors left the session of the council and later on left the university itself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters believe that those were Bosniak professors, but we're not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Just clarify this issue, as requested by the translator. Did the Muslim professors leave the university, or any others as well?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb professors had already left the university by that time. The Muslim professors left the university because their proposal was not accepted, namely to have the instruction held in Bosniak and Croatian languages in addition to the proposal about accepting a curriculum that would reflect humanitarian ideas and not claustrophobic ideas, which meant that the university would be shut to the outside world. Their ideas were not accepted under the circumstances, these ideas about a multinational university. As a result of that, 42 Bosniak professors left the university. We continued working in a different way. Our students who were enrolled at the university up until 1992, we examined them and we marked them with the traditional grading system, which was from 6 to 10, whereas the Croat professors continued teaching using the new Croatian curriculum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: One other question: When did this group of professors who were -- did not agree with the leadership of university try to solve this problem through the official Herceg-Bosna authorities? I mean not only the problem of university but the problem of the language as well.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: We established a Council of Muslim Intellectuals. This council was supposed to be some sort of an intellectual conscience of Mostar. We sent many appeals and many requests to put an end to this division in Mostar, this kind of an apartheid. Since the problems in Mostar were increasing, and there was also the resolution of the Herzegovina Muslims, and also the event when the Serbian Orthodox Church in Mostar was blown up, it was that that prompted us to draft a resolution attempting to protect the multi-cultural identity of Bosnia and attempting to ensure that it was only the legal organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina that would continue to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: By that time, Witness, were you aware of HDZ political, cultural programme?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It was quite obvious at every step. Wherever one went this programme led to intellectuals rallying round the Council of Intellectuals. We asked for a -- we looked for a creative solution aimed at preserving the cultural, ethnic identity of Mostar, of that town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What was the main goal put forward by your new association on your organisation of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: We drafted this resolution. A team started working on this resolution, and it was tasked with writing a draft resolution. Professor Zupcevic, university professor, was included into this effort, then myself, then Ico Mutevelic, who was a writer and a publicist, then the Mostar mufti Smajkic, and Adem -- I will remember his last name a bit later. We received the first version drafted by Ico Mutevelic, and we considered it at the meeting. Then I was tasked with providing a final version. When I gave the statement, I asked for the resolution to be given to me to refresh my memory, because I would like to inform the Trial Chamber about some of the details of the resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the registrar just to -- the witness to be shown Exhibit 00374. That will be page 2 English version, and page 1 B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, in your resolution - and you were one of the fathers of the resolution - you emphasised that you don't recognise any parastate of Croatians. What Croatians did you mean?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Under I, the third paragraph from below, it says that the Muslims are in favour of a whole and indivisible Bosnia and Herzegovina and will not recognise any parastate formations, in the plural. So the Bosniaks were not in favour of establishing Herceg-Bosna. And similar, they were against any other parastates, because the Serbs had established the SAO of Herzegovina, et cetera, the autonomous regions. Everyone is aware of fact. So we quite deliberately said that the Muslims were in favour of an integral Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we said that the Muslims would not recognise any parastates. Under number I, the second paragraph reads as follows: "We suggest that the Muslims live in harmony and love their honourable neighbours and fellow citizens, because there is no such thing as a collective sin, and therefore there is no such thing as collective responsibility. Every adult is responsible for himself and for his own acts."

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, my next question will be in paragraph I, page 3 of the English version, and page 1 in B/C/S version. You emphasised that Muslims seek the introduction of total equality for the Bosnian language, and so on, and you mentioned that 37 of the total inhabitants, according to the last census, declared themselves to be speakers. I would like to clarify. Did you mean only Muslims or all Yugoslavian people? Because it's not clear for me -- to me from the text of the resolution, especially the last part, with the Croatian and Serbian languages.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll read through the text: "The Muslims requesting full equality for the Bosnian language. 37 per cent of the inhabitants registered were in favour of this at the last census. They wanted to have equal status with Croatian and Serbian." What does this mean? It means that all those who used the Bosniak language, regardless of their nationality, should be fully equal with regard to those who call their own language the Croatian language or the Serbian language. So we were in favour of full equality for the Bosniak language. We weren't requesting that the Bosniak language have any exclusive rights. We wanted this language to be a language for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, it's a very delicate question, of course, because it's not the first trial here when the issue of the Bosnian language is discussed, and on many occasions the Defence raised the issue that the Bosnian language as such did not exist. What could you answer to this question?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber allows me to do this, I'd like to say that there was a delegation from this council composed of Ramiz Zupcevic, the president of the university, Professor Alija Piric, and the lawyer Damir Sadovic. And at the time, they visited the Prime Minister of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Jadranko Prlic at the time. I sent an original and a copy of a grammar book on the Bosnian language from 1890. I don't know whether he was provided with a copy of this grammar book. If not, I am quite prepared to send him a copy whenever he so requests. The Bosnian language, it's something I could give you a lecture on. I've given a hundred lectures on this matter. But the Bosnian language is the usual name used for the language used in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this grammar book is older than Maretic's grammar book on the Croatian language. It's made it possible -- it was made possible in 1991 for people to declare what language they used, and the Bosniak language was one possibility. 37 per cent of the population declared that the language they used was the Bosnian language. So this was an issue that was raised on a number of occasions. And at the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was also an issue that was discussed, because this term was abused, and the Croats called this language the Bosniak language --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Let's stop for a moment with linguistic problems and go back to the resolution. In paragraph 3 of the --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise. Is there something else I can add?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: That's enough for the moment.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... additional questions or the Defence will have questions, they will ask you, and the Judges as well. For the moment, the Prosecution is satisfied with your response. Witness, if you look at paragraph 3 of the resolution, this is page 4 English version and page 2 B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have it. Oh, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You don't have it on the screen? Do you have it now?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could it be enlarged, the part that your question will concern? I can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Is it possible? Yes. Do you see it now?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. Which part are you interested in?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Paragraph III. You say that you protest against any forms of military dictatorship and new fascism. What did you mean by these two very, very serious terms?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Could I see number III? I can see number IV and V. I can't see III. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Paragraph III. Paragraph III, page 2 of the B/C/S version. Do you see it now?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Could you explain? Could you answer my question about the dictatorship and neo-fascism you were protesting against.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: If the civilian population isn't allowed to move around freely, if some people wear the insignia of the fascists from the Second World War, if window screens have the photographs of Ante Pavelic in them, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the person you mentioned now? Explain, please, to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Ante Pavelic was the leader of a quisling creation, the Independent State of Croatia, during the Second World War. So if certain songs are sung about people who were fascists during the Second World War, if this is done on a massive scale, well, in that case we protested against such neo-fascism, against reviving such neo-fascism, and against any acts that were carried out in the spirit of fascism.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But what kind of people were wearing such kind of signs and singing such kind of songs?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the HOS and of the HVO would wear such insignia, and this was on a massive scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And in -- let's go to paragraph V. Paragraph V. This is page 5 of the English version, and page 2 B/C/S version. Do you see it, Witness?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I can see it, I've got it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I've got a question: In this paragraph you call on all Muslims fit for military service to join the ranks of defenders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Against whom? What did you mean to be ready for the defence? Against whom?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as you can see in this paragraph, it says: "We appeal to all those Muslims who were fit to serve in the military and who have not engaged yet to join the defenders of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then you can see what follows. It says that we're appealing to all such individuals to participate in the defence against the aggression, the Serbian aggression at the time. We didn't want them to join only the ranks of the BH army. We wanted them to join the ranks of the defenders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There are many Bosniaks who at the time were members of the HOS, the HVO, and the ABiH. We wanted them to commit themselves to the defence of their homeland.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Was this resolution made public?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: This resolution was made public. A number of press conferences were held with regard to this resolution, and I believe that it was published in certain newspapers, it was read out on Radio Mostar, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Was it easy for you to go back to Stolac after such kind of document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Naturally. I thought that this document was quite correct. I thought that it was a document that could be accepted by all people of goodwill, and I wasn't really afraid of returning to Stolac. I was afraid each time I returned there because sometimes there would be unpleasant experiences at the checkpoints. There were some threats, there were some disruptive people, but I always ignored it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, just one question: You were talking about "ausweiss", so-called permits to leave the territories of Stolac municipality. Was it applied to Croatia also? You could not go to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: You could only go to Croatia if you had received authorisation from Herceg-Bosna. If I wanted to go to Croatia, I had to receive authorisation from the relevant office in Stolac. Other documents issued by the legal bodies in Mostar - when I say "the legal bodies," I mean bodies loyal to the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina - these other documents were not recognised, and many people had problems when crossing the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And do you know where those "ausweiss" were printed, printed out?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: All the Herceg-Bosna documents were printed in Grude. And on all of the documents - and I was the director of a secondary school for many years, and as a result I know you have to have the year of printing on each document - on each document -- on each form, it said February, 1992. So this was two months prior to the declaration of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. School certificates, and these other documents were printed there as well as all other forms. All of these forms and documents were printed before Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared to be an independent state. Anyone who has such documents can check this. Children didn't want to take such documents, Bosniak children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, let's go to another part of questions. Somewhere in September, 1992, there was a meeting of representatives of Muslim's organisations and independent Muslim intellectuals in Mostar. Did you participate in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a meeting of representatives of all organisations involved in culture, education, science, religion, et cetera, et cetera. It was a meeting of all those who participated in social life at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: To what extent your resolution served the foundation document for this Council of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Council of Muslims wasn't an official institution. It was a coordinating body, or it was a body that coordinated institutions that existed at the time. It was a coordinating body that attempted to act in a coordinated way without posing a threat to anyone. They attempted to protect the interests of the Bosniaks who were at great risk at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit -- Prosecution Exhibit 09579. On page 1 in both versions. You see the name of Faruk Cupina. What was his official position and role in the organisation and functioning of this association?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, this is an excerpt from the minutes of that meeting. It was held on the 19th of September. 230 representatives from Mostar, Jablanica, Capljina, Konjic, Prozor, and other cities participated. There were other intellectuals from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Faruk Cupina and others presided over the meeting, and the Council of the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed there. Bitanga and Suta also presided. Faruk Cupina - you will see this later - was appointed as president of the Executive Board of that council at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And if you go further to this document, just analysis of the situation in Herzegovina. Page 1, we're dealing with items on the agenda. Could you briefly say, if you remember, of course, how did you assess the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time in September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: That was a situation in which it was necessary for us as intellectuals to state our position. That's why this Council of Intellectuals was formed, and then this coordinating council, because the constitutional and legal system of Bosnia and Herzegovina was at threat, was at risk. In September, the Constitutional Court rendered a decision according to which Herceg-Bosna was an entity that had been established counter to the constitution. So we were wondering what to do. We had to examine the situation and see how we could continue to cooperate. We had very serious problems with certain people at the time, certain people from the Party of Democratic Action who collaborated, cooperated with Herceg-Bosna and representatives from Herceg-Bosna. They were playing a sort of quisling role. We believed that it was necessary to take certain steps to protect the interests of the Bosniaks who were at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: In paragraph 7 - that's page 6 English version and page 2 B/C/S version - you express your protest "to the official organs of the Republic of Croatia over its refusal to recognise public documents of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at border crossings. Inform the official organs of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the contents of this protest." Did that kind of facts actually take place?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, such things did occur, and this could no longer be tolerated. A certain threshold had been crossed so it could no longer be tolerated. It was no longer a matter of individuals creating problems. At the time the border was practically closed for people who had legitimate documents from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Anyone who didn't have authorisation from Herceg-Bosna couldn't cross the Bosnian and Herzegovinian border, and that is why we lodged a protest with the government of Croatia and informed the bodies of our state of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you receive any feedback from the Croatian authorities? I mean the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we didn't. We had a public press conference at which we made all of these facts known, but unfortunately, no, we didn't receive any kind of feedback.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have finished with this set of questions, and I intend to pass on to another set of questions. Maybe it makes sense to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's time for the break, but for the sake of the transcript, the last document is 9579, whereas initially it was said 9779. So the number is 9579. We'll have our break now. It's now 20 to four, and we will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We are resuming our hearing. You can continue with examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, now we covered 1992 and let's pass on to 1993. How were you personally treated by the official Stolac authorities in 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, starting in 1993, in the very beginning of the year I had problems. I lived in my family house, and in April I had significant problems because they banned me from having any visitors in my house and I was banned from leaving my house, so in a way I was imprisoned in my own home. It was sort of a home detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Whose decision was it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The decision was written in the form of an order issued by a commander of the unit to which the unit which was in my brother's house in Begovina was subordinated. The document, the order, was signed by Veselin Veso Raguz. He was commander of that battalion. This order was affixed with a nail to the front door in Begovina. One can still see the nails on that door.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you file any complaint -- official complaint against any such kind of decision, such kind of arrest?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I immediately took a bicycle and rode to the command of that unit, to their headquarters. I found Mr. Raguza [as interpreted]. I was absolutely shocked to see that in the headquarters, in a room there, was a large picture of Ante Pavelic in the area where they used to hang a photograph of Josip Broz Tito. I protested very firmly and energetically, and I said that I wanted this to be clarified to me, that I was just an ordinary, loyal citizen. However, I received no explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, I would like you to clarify "Raguza." What was his position, and what is his first name? Mr. Raguz, to whom you turned to --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Veselin Veso Raguz, at the time, was in the commanding post of that battalion, which was in Stolac. Two months later, he was appointed commander of a unit that was in town, the unit that deported the residents of Stolac and sent them to concentration camps. Other remaining civilians, women, children, and the elderly, were driven out of that town. That's the man I am speaking of; Veselin Veso Raguz.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And so after this visit you remained after this home arrest. Until what time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the 1st of July, 5.00 a.m., when I was arrested and taken to Kostana hospital, or an orthopaedic hospital, which that year celebrated its 100th anniversary. I was taken to that hospital for a so-called informative interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Who arrested you, and who brought you to the hospital building?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: In the morning at 5.00 the soldiers came, the military police, with automatic rifles. They banged on the door. I woke up, opened the door for them. The only thing they allowed me to do was put my jeans on, Adidas shoes, and a T-shirt. And this is how I went to have this interview which, unfortunately, lasted for several months.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And were there any arrests before the 1st of July in Stolac? I mean, arrests of the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the reason I was put under house arrest was that on the 20th of April, the entire crew of civilian protection was arrested. All Muslims. They were not Croats. They were taken to a camp in Grabovo near Capljina. At the time a unit which was an ally of the HVO, a brigade which was in the vicinity of Stolac was disarmed, and one must know that this legal brigade was unable to cross into the territory of the town of Stolac. It was at a distance of some 20 to 30 kilometres but was not allowed to cross into the territory of Stolac proper. It was at that time that the entire brigade was disarmed and taken to prison, together with all of the members of the civilian protection. I can give the names of the people who were taken on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: First of all, I would like you to clarify the name of the brigade, because it's missing in the record, in the transcript. What was the name of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The brigade was called Bregava Brigade. It was the brigade of defenders from Stolac, and it was named after the river which passes through -- which runs through our town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Was it a pure Muslim unit or mixed unit?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It was a Muslim unit. I think that it had two or three Serb members.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And you were talking about some names. Who was commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of that unit was Bajro Pizovic, a teacher. Staff Commander, and his deputy was Colonel Dzemil Sijacic. Mehmed Dizdar was arrested on that occasion, and the entire commanding cadre, including Sacir Turkovic, who was from civilian protection, another teacher, a Muslim teacher, and then Ibrahim Mahmutovic, also a teacher. They tried to arrest the intellectuals, the educated people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what was Mehmed Dizdar's position?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mehmed Dizdar was, before the war, deputy police chief. And this also was so while the Serbs were in Stolac. After that, he had serious problems. He had to go into hiding because the HVO threatened to kill him. He went for a few days to HOS and from there he went to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and was a member of the command staff. He wrote a book about his experiences there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Were there any other facts of arrest at the beginning of July, 1993, in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian name for the month of July is Srpanj. The word "srp" denotes a scythe that is used to cut wheat or grass. It was then that all male residents from Stolac under the age of 65 were taken to Dretelj, Heliodrom, and other places. I was arrested among the first one. I was the second or third to be arrested. And then, following that, others were arrested as well. I myself was sent to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what about members of your family and your close relatives? Were they arrested?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, all members of my extended family, those who happened to be in Stolac, were arrested and taken to camps. My brother, who resides in the Netherlands nowadays, was taken to the notorious tunnel in the camp, which I'm sure will be mentioned later. So all of the members of my extended family were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what about your wife?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: My wife and my daughter remained in the house after I was taken alone with some 30 soldiers. My wife didn't know what was going to happen to me. She tried to get in touch with people in town. She tried to go to the command headquarters to inquire about my fate. Nobody wanted to talk to her. She could see that something serious was going on. She came back home quite anxious. Several days later, upon receiving some information from acquaintances of ours that I was in Dretelj, she came to see me there, trying to bring some clothing for me and other things. She came back on the 10th of July, and after that she was no longer allowed to go back to our house. She then took up residence with our neighbours some 200 to 300 metres from Begovina. And for some three or four days she would go to our house during daytime, and following that, she was completely banned from entering our house. Both she and our daughter were banned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what happened to her later in 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of August of that year, 1993, all residents of Stolac who remained living there - the elderly, women, children, the infirm - all of them were loaded onto trucks and taken to factories, schools, and were deported from there to the separation line near Mostar, near Buna, several kilometres from the town of Blagaj. From there she, together with her old and elderly parents, walked for several kilometres every day. Her mother could not -- no longer continue. She was very exhausted. A lot of the elderly were killed on that road, because they used to fire at them. And then a young man appeared, and he used a wheelbarrow, a construction wheelbarrow in order to transport my mother-in-law for the remaining portion of that trip. She was 80 years old. Only 16 Bosniaks remained in Stolac out of 5.000 something. You saw the statistics yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: From whom did you hear this information about the circumstances under which your wife and other people from Stolac were deported?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I received first information while in Dretelj. Some people were in hiding, and some 10 to 15 people came into the hangar where I was, and they told us that everybody had been deported from Stolac. So I learned about her fate while in Dretelj. I didn't know anything about my son for several months, though. And what made it especially hard for me was that in his hangar there were some 15 schoolmates of my son, 15 and 16-year-olds, children who were imprisoned in camp together with me. There were also some elderly people there, including Hamdija Mesak, who was over 80 at the time. I described him at length in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And let's go back to your arrest and the hospital building. How long -- for how long were you kept there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Once I arrived in the hospital, I asked to meet with the military police commander, Mr. Puljic. He was a mechanical engineer. He used to go to the high school where I was a principal. I thought that he didn't know what was going on, so I thought I should inform him. As soon as I mentioned that, I received a blow with a fist in my jaw. They broke my jaw on that occasion, and I was taken to the basement of the hospital, and I spent some two or three hours there - I'm not quite sure, but around two or three hours - following which I was deported together with another two men, Esad Suta, and another one who told me that this would not last for a long time because his school friend Valenta Coric would interfere as they were school friends. The other man was called Camil Medar. I believe that he was an economist. They drove us in a closed van. The driver and the person escorting us were armed. These two young men used to greet each other with this gesture throughout that trip. I came to the gate of Dretelj, and I was there taken to Ivica Kraljevic. He started creating a list of all of those who were brought there. He took my personal ID, and after that I didn't have a single ID on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what was his position? I mean, Ivica Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Ivica Kraljevic was deputy commander or deputy warden of the camp in Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: How many people were brought along with you to Dretelj on that day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: On that day and on the following day, a total of 3.500 to 3.600 of people were brought there. Why did I say on the following day? Because on the following day the HVO soldiers came, and these were Muslims, Bosniaks, members of the HVO. That was a unique event where, without any kind of an armed rebellion, soldiers of an organisation, of a military organisation, were disarmed and arrested. They were brought there directly from front lines. Front lines facing the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Professor, but at the time when you were brought to Dretelj, were you interrogated by anyone, any officials of the camp?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody interrogated me. They took me immediately to a makeshift building, house, which was used as a storage for fuel and for oil. Everything was dirty, smeared with fuel and oil, based on which I concluded that this facility was used as a storage. On the floor we had only concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who was commander of Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the man. I saw him. I think that his name was Anicic. Later on, Tomo Sakota was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who was providing security to the camp? I mean on the perimeter of the camp Dretelj, by whom was it guarded?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And do you know who --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I saw only military police when I came there. I don't know whether there was anybody else there. Later on, I had no occasion to go out and see. But those who guarded us, whom I could see, were military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And those who were guarding you within the camp were also from military police or from any other HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the people I'm referring to. I believe that they were military policemen. I didn't pay too much attention to their insignia. At the time, it was not important for me. They were definitely, though, members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And on one occasion you mentioned a person, Valentin Coric, who could help one of the prisoners or persons who was arrested along with you. Did you know his position at that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't. I didn't know the man from before. I had no contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who told you that it was possible to help another inmate how to get away from the arrest?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, various letters of guarantee arrived from all over Europe, from friends who had been residing abroad for many years. Based on those letters of guarantee, very rarely they would let somebody out. So an insignificant number of people were fortunate enough to leave the concentration camp. Naturally, I attempted to send a message to my sister to have her try something similar. Unfortunately, it was useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Where were you kept in Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: In Dretelj I was in a makeshift house. I told you what it had been used before. It had a huge door. I assume that they needed this huge door to bring in the fuel in containers. This building had four or five windows, I'm not sure exactly how many. They were 1.5 by 0.5 metres with iron bars on them. There was glass in the windowpane. Later on we had to break the glass in order to have some air. This makeshift house had a very light type of roof called Salonit, and we were there in that empty building lying on a cement floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And how many people were detained in that barrack?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I never counted the people, but I know this: Somehow we could manage to sit down, but the only way to lie down was for all of us to lie on our sides. To this day, I have black marks on both sides of my body. There would be 50 people in one row. Once our bodies became numb, and if we wanted to turn to another side, all of us had to turn at the same time. There were many rows of people, and one can actually do the math to see how many people there were there altogether. For a long time, I had bruises on both sides of my pelvis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And how many barracks were there in Dretelj complex?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there were seven such areas where about 3.500 people were kept. I think there were five makeshift houses and two tunnels. We called them tunnels because those were entrances into subterranean storages that had no exit on the other side. So this was just a huge storage area, and above them were bars plus the door, which was five to six metres wide. And those openings were the only openings through which the air came to the people who were in the tunnel. My brother was in one such tunnel and I was in a makeshift house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what categories of detainees were detained in Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They were all detained. There were no exceptions. The worst thing was that there were children there. Perhaps it's because I've spent my entire life with children that that affected me. Perhaps it was because my son went to school with them, but that's something I will never forget. That's an image that will never fade from my memory. They grew thinner from day to day. Their eyes grew larger, their ears grew larger; everything else grew smaller. So these people were there, and there was some elderly people in the place that I was detained in. The others were citizens who weren't members of any military units. The soldiers who were in the HVO were in the tunnels, and they fared the worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And your brother was also member of the HVO? Sorry. Yes, former member of HVO or not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. He was a member of the civilian protection. He came to see my wife, to find out what had happened to me. When they were disarming troops that were in my brother's house, they collected him. He also went see his father in flip-flops, and he was wearing some sort of a sports T-shirt, and that's how he appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Were there any elderly people within the Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were elderly people there, from the age of 65 and over. There were quite a few of them. I saw a number of them in my shack, in my hut. I saw someone called Hamdija Mesak, who is a neighbour of mine, also a godfather. It's a long story. There was this elderly man who was 83 years old who looked very miserable in that situation. There was another agronomist, Mizo Dizdar, and every morning he would raise his hand and say, "Sir, I'm an engineer of agronomy. Can I go to my site because if the wind blows, the vines will be ruined." So imagine a person involved in cultivation, the cultivation of such things to find himself in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So, Witness, did you have enough water within your barrack?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we didn't have water or food. Once a day we would receive something that they called lunch. 33 aluminum pots would be placed on the floor. 33 aluminum containers would be placed on the asphalt. And they'd fill all these pots up from a large container. It was water with a bit of pasta or a couple of beans inside. We would take it in turns, and on each occasion 11 of us would go out and receive this ration. Six hundred grams of bread would be divided into 16 portions. Try and imagine this. So that amounted to two or three mouthfuls of bread. After we had drunk that hot food, because we had 17 minutes to have that so-called lunch, after which we'd go and drink water, and that's all the water we would get. My mouth, my lips, my throat were constantly irritated. I no longer had a mucous membrane. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what about toilet facilities? Did you have any?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, for a very long time it's not just that we didn't have a toilet to use, but we just weren't provided with the possibility of leaving the hangar to relieve ourselves. So what did we do? Sometimes someone would bring a bag of some kind or a plastic bottle, a plastic bottle of Coca-Cola, et cetera, or whatever they would find in the hangar. We would urinate into those bottles, and at night we'd pour the contents out through the broken windows. When we had to defecate, we would use those bags, and at night we would throw those bags out of the windows. That was one of the most humiliating things that we experienced there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you receive any medical assistance?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: After a certain period of time, there was a shack that was used to keep fire extinguishers in before, and something like a clinic was established there. Let's call it that. And there was a doctor who was also a camp detainee who was taken there. And when it was necessary to provide people with first aid, that's where they were taken to. This doctor had very little -- very few medical supplies at his disposal. The facilities were terrible. It was something that existed there more for the sake of -- of form. It was pro forma.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now, I would like to pass on to some exhibits. Is it proper to put hard copies to the witness or to use e-court system? Which is better? Hard copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try to provide the witness with an electronic version of the document. If it doesn't work, we'll use the ELMO. Could you please provide us with the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. First exhibit, that's 9019. It has two pictures with digit numbers 01092986, 01092987. 86, not 68. I repeat: 01092986. Page 10 of the album.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would probably be best to use the ELMO. We'll place the photographs on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's quicker this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. First photo. Witness, do you recognise this place? Have you ever been there before?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Dretelj. If I can point this out. Well, you can see the tunnel here. And these are the shacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Which one is the shacks?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a shack, and this is the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: This is the tunnel here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: -- you to mark just the tunnel by encircling it with the marker. And put number 1, your initials, and the date.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes, the date. Your initials. You should put the date just inside the circle. You might.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And your initials.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I've done that. You've got my initials there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And the barrack should be circled as well. Put number 2.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. I think that that will be enough with this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 9564.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see this exhibit, Witness?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. This is the shack that I was detained in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Which one? There are three.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: To the right you can see the shack that I marked with number 2 just a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Just -- you may mark it now with number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Again, we should --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: On the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: No. You should mark the barrack, not the sky.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your initials.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I would like the registrar to capture these exhibits and give them e-court numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
