utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, we need some exhibit numbers. The first one that was on the ELMO should be dealt with first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... will be allocated the -- assigned, sorry, the Exhibit IC 00012. The second exhibit marked on the e-court system will be assigned the Exhibit IC 00013. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, when did you meet your brother in the Dretelj camp first?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it was a month and a day later at this place where they would distribute lunch. Well, my brother came from this direction, I came from the direction of the shacks. We met quite by chance. That was the only way we could have met. When I saw him, I didn't recognise him until he was only a metre and a half or two metres away from me. And when he approached me, there was mould, green mould, on his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What is his name, your brother?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: His name is Smail Rizvanbegovic. He's a civil engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, were you visited by the Red Cross at an occasion in Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Red Cross representatives came on one occasion. This is referred to in documents that I have provided to you. It's referred to in a Red Cross certificate. They visited the camp, and that was the first time that we met someone from the outside. They spent a number of days examining us. They measured our height. They weighed us. I have documents to support the claim that I was 60 -- I weighed 64 kilogrammes at the time, whereas I weighed 87 when I first arrived in the camp. It also says that I was 1 metre 82 centimetres tall. So I was just skin and bones.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 0996.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Just -- is it -- do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Then I would like the witness to be provided with --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. Now do you see it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it now. That's the identification document that I received from the Red Cross at the time. And I could remember the number of my personal identity card which I jotted down on this certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And if you turn to the second page of this document. Do you see --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was talking about. They wrote down the weight and height of the individuals that they registered. This was done by official representatives of the Red Cross. I weighed 64 kilos, and my height was 1 metre 82 centimetres. And they did this for all those whom they examined. And I do believe that they examined everyone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did they have enough time to talk to each of you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They spent several days there. And the certificate that I received in Zagreb after I had left the camp, it mentions the date of their visit and how long they stayed there. They were not able to speak to all of us, that would have required far more time, but during the several days that they spent there, they did speak to a certain number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 7366. Do you see the document, Witness?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a certificate that I requested in Zagreb. I wanted to have some form of identification so that I could move around Zagreb. I went to the Red Cross and to the UNHCR. You can see the dates here. It says that I was visited regularly from the 6th of September until the 15th of September, 1993. That's when they came and visited us in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And I see that the document was issued on the 28th of December, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's when it was issued. At the time, I was already in Zagreb, and that's when I went to the Red Cross to obtain some kind of a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come back to this document a little bit later when we will talk about a different topic. And now about the treatment of inmates in the Dretelj camp. How were you treated by the people who were guarding the camp and who were attending you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it really was a concentration camp. As you have already heard, the food we were provided with was such as I have already described it. On one day I had a mouthful of bread, and I had another small piece of bread in my other hand. The guard who saw that I had held onto a little piece of bread in my hand asked me what I had in my hand. I said I had a piece of bread. He hit me so hard with his rifle that I fell onto the concrete a few metres away from him, on the concrete that we saw in front of those shacks a minute ago. And he said, "Balija, don't you know you should say 'kruh' and not 'sreb.'" I will explain this. In the Croatian language, "kruh" is the word for bread, and in the Bosnian language, you use both words; you would use the word "kruh" and "sreb." I couldn't get up because I had no more air in my lungs. He asked me what I did, what my profession was. I said I was a professor, and that's when he really got angry. He put me down on the floor, and it was 1.00 p.m. He put me down on the scorching ground because it was mid-July, 1993, and then he said I had to stare at the sun. I did so for a while, and then I could no longer keep my eyes open. My eyes started fluttering. He put his leg on my chest then. He put his rifle to my forehead, and he said, "If you blink once more, I'll kill you. You will no longer need your eyes." And I really stared at that summer sun for so long that I went totally blind. He then called to the men to take me inside. And when they took me inside, the white part of my eye was completely bloody, and you couldn't distinguish the pupil from the rest of the eye. And this isn't something that I alone experienced. This was done to another young man, Saric, who is now the director of Norfis [phoen]. This is one drastic example of the way in which they treated an ordinary detainee. But there were others who received special treatment, and there were many of them whose cries we heard and whom we saw. I will mention a few names. There was the president of the Islamic Community, Alija Festic. He was also 65 years old. And he was so badly beaten that his neck was wider than his head. You couldn't see his eyes. His lips were completely bloated. Then there was someone called Maric, also known as Zenga. I could mention many other names, but I don't want to waste your time, because many individuals were treated in this cruel way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, just one question: Were the guards of the camp all the time within the barracks alone with the detainees?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They were never in the shacks with the detainees. They would appear in the morning, they would open the big doors, three or four of them would stand there. There would be the guard commander in the middle. He would appear, raise a finger like this without saying anything, and all the detainees inside had to sing a song, a fascist song from the Second World War: "Here's the dawn, here is Jure Boban." And it refers to Ante Pavelic, the leader, and these other two criminals from the Second World War also well known. He would raise his hand like this and we would have to sing the song, then he would put his hand down and we'd have to stop singing the song. He'd raise two fingers again and we'd have to sing a different song. "Sarajevo is beneath Trebovic and we will have Ante Pavelic again." I'll never forget that song. When he put his hand down again, there was silence, and then he would raise his hand for a third time and he'd raise three fingers in the air, and we would then have to sing, "I don't like you Alija because you are a balija. The Drina will take you away and some Mujahedin will be taken away every day." We would have to sing that song every morning for a long time. And that's what they did. They'd go from one shack to the other, and everyone had to sing all these songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, were you ever visited by any officials of Herceg-Bosna authorities?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, only once. A delegation came comprising representatives not only of Herceg-Bosna but also the Republic of Croatia. Minister of foreign affairs of Croatia came, Mate Granic, then Mr. Jadranko Prlic, Mr. Soljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Prlic, what position was he held at that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: While I was free, he was Prime Minister of the government of Herceg-Bosna. I suppose that he held the same office when he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And did they communicate with the detainees?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They passed through the camp. They spoke to some of the detainees. One of them was Emir Mrgan and Mr. Prlic set him free on that day. Then two days later he was brought back. Whether this was coincidental or staged, I can't say. At any rate, they saw all of us, they spoke to some of us. They saw what we looked like. One glance was sufficient to know exactly what was going on there. Tomo Sakota had voluminous documentation about the camp. He moved through the camp, taking pictures of us, and I think that this should be with him, or with somebody else, the documentation. On that occasion when he walked around with this delegation, he also had a camera on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you know Jadranko Prlic before?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: We knew each other to the extent that both of us were professors at the Mostar university. Prior to that, Prlic was deputy president of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, back in the old days. So we knew each other through the efforts to improve the teaching at the university. There were various projects at the university. So we knew each other to the extent that people know each other when they work at the same university.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did he recognise you in Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: You should ask him that. I don't think that he was unable to see me, because I tried to stand as close as possible to the fence, the yellow one that you saw on the screen just a minute ago. I think that he was able to see me. Unfortunately, he didn't pay attention to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did they enter the barracks and the tunnels?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They took us to stand in front of the shacks. Everybody sat on the ground, on the asphalt, and they passed next to the people. Now, as to whether they entered some of the empty shacks, I think they did, but I think you need to ask the gentlemen about that. At any rate, they saw the conditions under which we were kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did ever representatives of the mass media visit Dretelj while you were kept there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Not until then. Some media representatives came with that delegation. A notorious journalist, Lovrenovic, came with them. He even got on a big boulder and held -- gave a speech. As though it wasn't enough that he wrote terrible articles prior to that, he also gave us a speech, a horrible speech. I think that CNN broadcast some footage or a picture from the camp. My sister, who had previously spent some time in Capljina as a doctor, was in Norway, and she saw that on CNN. She taped that footage, because my brother was in that shot. Whether other media outlets reported on this, I don't know. I was locked in. But it would be sufficient to just glance through several issues of Slobodna Dalmacija from that time to see what a terrible machinery it was, the propaganda machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: You mentioned that Slobodan Lovrenovic wrote some terrible articles. Please, could you explain what kind of horrors were described in his articles.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Later on I read that. At the time, I was unable to read it. Although, before I went to the camp he had already been active writing warmongering texts. He was always one of the journalists who generated hatred among ethnic communities. In all of his texts, he accused us camp inmates for being camp inmates. This would be his position in a nutshell. I think that you can find his articles in various libraries and so on. I think it's very easy to see what the reaction of Croatian media was at the time, especially reaction of Slobodan Lovrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: One question: Could you recall whether that Mr. Jadranko Prlic's visit to the Dretelj camp was performed after or before the Red Cross visit?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say that with certainty, but it would be easy to establish that because it was recorded by the media. You see the date in my ICRC ID. So it's easy to establish that. It happened within a few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Before or after?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't say with certainty. I wouldn't dare to give you an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Again, one question: Were you ever interrogated in the Dretelj camp by some investigator?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Never. Nothing ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did they explain to you for what reason you, a civilian person, were being kept for so long time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, all of us were civilians. Even the disarmed soldiers, after being disarmed, were treated as civilians. So all of us inside were civilians. They had absolutely no reason to explain anything to us. If you inquired about something, there was always a danger of them killing you, beating you up, breaking your ribs, splitting your head open. If they asked you something, it didn't really matter what you answered. If you said yes, then they would say to you, "Balija, why did you do that?" If you answered no, then they would say, "Balija, why didn't you do that?" So it really didn't matter what we answered. And the general system was such that nobody received ever any kind of an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what happened to your brother? How did he manage to get released from the camp, from the Dretelj camp?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: We received a letter from my sister-in-law, who is from Slovakia. I have two sisters-in-law because I have two brothers. One of them is a Serb lady, and the other one is a lady from Slovakia. The lady from Slovakia sent me letter. My other sister-in-law was staying with her at the time. So they sent a hear from Hana's parents, a letter of guarantee for him to be able to leave. This letter reached us via Zagreb. My name was also in that letter. My name was ignored. And as for my brother, he wasn't released. Rather, on the 20th of August, I believe, he was transferred from Dretelj in order not to be found there, and transferred to Gabela. Transferred from Dretelj to Gabela. He remained in Gabela even after the Dretelj camp was closed down. I think that he was set free on the 23rd of November, set free from Gabela. This letter that reached us on the 20th -- this letter reached us on the 20th of August, and I left on the 10th of December. I have a stamp in my documents, and you can see on which date I left. As I said, the letter reached us on the 20th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see that letter in Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. One day they called me in to tell me that a letter had arrived. Then they showed a list of 64 names that may absolutely not be released. This list contained the names of 64 intellectuals. Unfortunately, later on I realised that this list was an authentic one, because all of the people from that list were later on transferred to the prison in Ljubuski. I was on that list, too, and I was also transferred to the prison in Ljubuski after the camp in Dretelj was closed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I asked you about the document where your brother name and your name was included. When did you see it first?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it when Tomo Sakota brought it to me in Ljubuski. That was a document with which I was supposed to cross the border of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was on the 10th of December. Prior to that, it had been concealed from me. However, you have that document in -- you have that letter in your documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to be shown Exhibit 4366.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see it now?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the document. The 20th of August, 1993. And then it says here, "On the 14th of October, 1993, border crossing in Metkovici," which is where my brother crossed the border. And then below it is the date of the 10th of December, when I crossed the border. So the upper date is the one when my brother was released, and the other one is when I was released. I apologise. It wasn't November, it was, rather, October. And this document is signed by Adalbert Rebic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And where did your brother leave for?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: My brother went to Croatia, to Zagreb, and then from Zagreb he went to Slovakia. From there he went to Germany, to my sister-in-law's uncle, and then from there they came to the Netherlands, which is where they reside now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did he go to Slovakia alone or with his family?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: His family had left prior to that, when they received an invitation from my sister-in-law. So they were already in Slovakia, his son and his wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember the circumstances in which you left Dretelj?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think the term "left" is an inappropriate one. They put handcuffs on me, and then they took me to a completely closed van without any windows. Another two men were brought in. One was president of the Islamic Community, Alaga Fetic that I mentioned to go a bit ago, and Esad Suta.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like to clarify his name because you just told us a different name. Festic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Who else?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Esad Suta. Then they took us to the camp in Gabela. They were supposed to fetch some other people there, but they didn't find them there. So it was just the three of us who were taken to a place that we didn't know. We didn't know where we were going, because the van was closed, without windows. So we didn't know where we were being taken. It was only several days later that we learned we were in the Ljubuski prison. Several days later, they took us outside of the prison perimeter, and then they took me to the solitary confinement cell, which was completely dark. I didn't know whether it was day or night-time. There was nothing in it except for the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: How many people were taken to Ljubuski? Please repeat. Repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I was unable to know for a long time how many people were in Ljubuski, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: No, no, Witness. I meant this time when you were transferred from Dretelj to Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It was just the three of us on that occasion, just the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They told us that there should be another two men with us. We were told this by the drivers, but we didn't know who these other two men were supposed to be. I think that later on we heard that Maric, the person whom I mentioned who had been beaten a lot, and somebody else were supposed to be these additional two men. However, they were not taken there with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know the date when you were taken to Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 23rd of September; the date when the camp in Dretelj was being shut down. They decided not to release us from the camp because those were instructions from the international community. Instead, they got all of us intellectuals and they took us to the prison in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you know whose order it was to transfer to Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I suppose that the order came from the chief of the military police, because that was a military prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like witness to be shown Exhibit 5312.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can see who signed it: Mr. Valentin Coric. I can also see that it says here that I should be taken there with the utmost security measures en route and transferred to Ljubuski. The security measures were indeed successful. I was tied up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what about the names which are indicated there? Are all familiar to you or not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I was the president of the cultural society, Preporod. Alija Festic was president of the Islamic community of Stolac, and Ahmed Habota and Esad Suta were in the SDA party. One of them was the chairman of the party in our region and the other one was president of the Executive Board. As for Salko Maric, I think I mentioned him before to you as the man who was severely beaten so that his head was twice the size. I think his nickname is Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay. Let's now pass on to the Ljubuski prison. So, as you have just explained to the Trial Chamber, on the day when you were transferred there, you were put into the solitary cell. Could you describe the witness in that solitary cell.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I told you that there was nothing in it. I sat on the floor. Frequently they would intimidate me. They constantly were fumbling with the keys and opening or unlocking and locking the door. There was constantly that type of noise. On one occasion, two men came, opened the door. One of them started yelling at me. I was taken aback. He was yelling and saying they would do this to me and that to me. And then he took a pistol out, and he shoved it into my mouth. And he shoved it so deep that all of a sudden I vomited. And he pulled back his pistol unexpectedly and broke two of my teeth. When I came to Zagreb, I went to the dental school there, and they created some kind of a temporary solution for me. When I threw up, some of the contents of it landed on his shoes, and then he started yelling so hard and took the pistol and hit me right here in my jaw and broke the teeth in this area. So that was one of the events in that prison. I can tell you about another event, extraordinary event and extraordinary man. Rudolf Jozelic was a pilot --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, we'll pass on to this person later on, but right now let's finalise the situation with the solitary cell. Did they give food to you, water?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It was similar to the situation in Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: For how long did they keep you in the solitary cell?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think for a few days. I'm not sure. As I told you, I didn't know about the time of the day, but I think I stayed there for several days. After that, they transferred me to another cell where there were seven of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Who was there in the next cell? Do you know those people?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I do. Several days before they transferred me to this other cell, they brought another man from Stolac, Mirsad Mahmutcehajic. He came into my cell, so for a while there were two of us in that cell and then they transferred me to another cell where there were seven of us: Rudi Jozelic, Esad Suta, Alija Festic. People were gathered there from different solitary confinement cells. So there was Alija Festic, Mehmed Zilic. Those were the men who were there with me. The conditions there were a bit better. I didn't lie on concrete floor; rather, there were some mattresses there, and we lay next to each other, crammed in like sardines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, sometime before, just you mentioned some names, some list of detainees which you saw in the Dretelj camp with some names which were familiar to you. I would like witness to be shown -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 7785.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see this list?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Are any of the names indicated in that list familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know almost all of the names, because these are people that I know. Most of them. You can see for yourself these are all doctors, professors. Intellectuals, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Whom you know the best of all these detainees?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I know most of these people. Dr. Muhamed Kapic was director of the Kostana hospital. Mahmutcehajic went to school with me. Zijo Demirovic was an architect. Mehmed Zilic is a relative of my wife. I think that he had a position in the army or, rather, in the Territorial Defence. He worked there. Rudolf Jozelic was a pilot. I don't know Alija Demirzic. I know Hamdija Jahic. I have know Dr. Esad Boskailo. I know Professor Mehmed Dizdar, I know Veledar, I know Vlado Fink, I know Professor Ragib Dizdar. I know most of the people here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: That's enough. Were all these people kept in Ljubuski along with you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of them were in various cells in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you happen to see them during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime towards the second half of my stay in Ljubuski they used to take us out for some kind of a prison walk. They would let us walk around in the yard with our hands on our backs. We were not allowed to talk among each other. Then after this five-minute walk, we had to stand against the wall. Mr. Jozelic would be taken out then every day and put in the middle of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I tell you about it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes. We have a few minutes before the technical break.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rudolf Jozelic, Rudi, was in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He used to be a pilot before the war. They would take him out every day. If the nationality is of any importance, and it was at that time, well, his nationality was Croatian. They were taken to the middle of the grounds, and then they would ask him whether he had changed his mind; would he transport Alija Izetbegovic or Franjo Tudjman in a plane? He wouldn't reply. Then they would tell him to do push-ups, he would then do them, and then they'd tell him to fly and they'd humiliate him. He'd have to spread out his arms, run around in a circle, and when he arrived at the end he had to pretend to be turning around in an aeroplane. The humiliation of an honourable man was endless. When he was exhausted, when he could no longer run around, he would fall down and they would usually kick him in the face. He was wearing some sort of a tracksuit covered in blood, a grey tracksuit, and blood would drip onto it. He was bleeding in the face. And this went on for a few days. It's something that is hard to believe. This was done before all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now I think it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's time for the break. How much longer do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like to finalise my examination-in-chief today, but I cannot promise you, Your Honour. Maybe I'll leave some time for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's half past five now. We will resume at ten to six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, there is a question that the Chamber would like to put to you. One hour and a half had been scheduled for this witness, so you have already used twice that amount of time, three hours for your examination-in-chief. As Defence counsel will have the same amount of time as you had, that means that with regard to the other witnesses tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, and on Thursday, it will be necessary to shorten the length of time for their examination. I see Mr. Mundis nodding. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As Mr. Scott has indicated on a couple of prior occasions, these estimates are simply that, estimates. We are well aware of the time limitations placed on all of the parties, and we will, of course, do what is necessary to ensure that the witnesses that are scheduled for this week are completed this week, and if that means making reductions in the two remaining witnesses, we of course will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas. It is not necessary to intervene right now because this is a problem that concerns the Prosecution. The Prosecution has just said that they will reschedule their witness. Unless you want to say that you prepared yourself for an hour and a half and now you have three hours. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, all I can say, Mr. President, is every Thursday the Defence feels squeezed. We will not be squeezed any more because the Prosecution is taking more time. So if they can't finish their witnesses, their witnesses may have to stay over the weekend. I'm telling that because they know their witnesses better than we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Mundis, Mr. Karnavas has pointed out that there is this problem. It's true that when we have a schedule and when we expect a witness to be examined for an hour and a half, everyone prepares on that basis, prepares for an hour and a half of examination. But in this case we see that you've almost doubled the time you require for your examination-in-chief. So this can cause a problem, and Mr. Karnavas's objection is quite legitimate. But it could have been done when it was time for Defence counsel to commence with their cross-examination. Very well. You may proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanbegovic, who was the camp commander in Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Ivica Kraljevic was the commander for a certain period of time, but when I arrived there, I don't know who the commander was. I think it was Ivica Kraljevic. I'm certain it was Ivica Kraljevic for a certain period of time because he interrogated me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And do you remember the circumstances of that interrogation? What questions were you asked?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: On two or three occasions I was taken to a room where they interrogated me, where Ivica interrogated me. Two armed soldiers took me there. They would stand behind me when Ivica spoke to me. There were two other men in military uniforms. They were sitting there. The questions put to me were almost totally insignificant. Ivica kept repeating that he had a lot of documents on me, et cetera, et cetera, but he never put any questions that had much sense to me. At one point in time I asked him, "What are you accusing me of?" He said, "For destroying the constitutional order of Herceg-Bosna." I laughed. He asked me why, and I said, "Herceg-Bosna is not a constitutional entity. I cannot destroy something that doesn't exist." I think that was the last time I was interrogated. I think it was a quite insignificant event, so I really didn't really have problems of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: But were the investigators taking any written notes of your statement or not, or was it a verbal interrogation?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think that these two men took notes of some kind, but I don't know what they did. Ivica didn't take any notes. He just spoke to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you affix any signature to any of your witness statements?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, you informed the Trial Chamber that you were released from Ljubuski on the 10th of December, 1993. Could you just explain, how did you manage to get released from Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: My sister was first in Graz [as interpreted] and then Hvar and then Zagreb, did everything she could. The other sister, not the doctor. She did everything she could to contact my friends in Croatia, because I did have a lot of friends in Croatia. That's where I studied, that's where I did my post-graduate studies and where I obtained my doctorate. Ivo Franges, the late Ivo Franges, the academic, was someone who supported me in particular, and Dunja Falisevac, who studied with me and was the chief of the literature, supported me, and there were other people who supported me. They wrote requests and sent them to President Tudjman's office. One day I received some information from my sister through certain individuals who were in touch with her. I don't know what channels were used exactly to establish such contact, but these were people who provided me with information. I don't know them, they never introduced themselves, but they said that all their requests had been useless because there were some people who had a flat in Mostar -- or someone said I had a flat in Mostar with a lot of ammunition. I was surprised by this. I never had such a flat in which I'd kept ammunition, but my wife had the address of my relative in America, Suad Rizvanbegovic, and his wife is a friend of the governor of Grenada, and that person is a friend with Galbraith, so they then informed the American ambassador in Zagreb, and I think that that is how they first -- I first obtained support. And then there was this group of intellectuals that had links with a literary association in Croatia, and they launched an initiative which bore fruit, I think. And in the end, I was released on the 10th of December. When I met them, they were all surprised by the way I looked and they all supported me and I'm now on extremely friendly terms with all those who supported me at the time and with all those who didn't even know the sort of situation I was in at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: On what condition were you released from Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Tomo Sakota arrived. He brought that piece of paper, the document that we saw on the screen a while ago. He also appeared with another document, an authorisation for my release. And then went to Capljina with these documents. Tomo took me to our friend Zdenka, who unfortunately wasn't at home. But my alternative was to go to her friend's place if she wasn't there. That's where I went. I had a bath. I had a lot of lice. All the detainees in Dretelj and later in Ljubuski had a lot of lice, so they had to shave our heads. After I had had a bath, I was provided with a JNA uniform. That's what they provided us with when it was cold. My sister then sent some clothes that I put on. I then went to Gradac and then to Split, and she found a German in Split who took me to Zagreb by plane. I stayed with my aunt's daughter, and she had provided me with a guarantee for my stay in Zagreb. My friends then helped me, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Sir, you were released, as far as I understood, on condition that you would travel somewhere from Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I was released, and I was to travel to some third country. The idea was that I should go to Germany. While I was in Ljubuski, I found out that my son was -- well, he was first in Slovakia and with our friends, with friends of my sister-in-law Hana. There were too many of them there, so then a friend of mine from Banja Luka took him to Berlin, and then I went to see my son in Berlin, but I saw that that was senseless. As an intellectual it wasn't for me to go abroad. It was for me to stay in Bosnia. So I got in contact with Enes Durakovic, the minister of education, and I told him that I wanted to return to Sarajevo. I waited for two or three -- two or three months in Zagreb, and finally I arrived in Sarajevo. I didn't want to go abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, and who made the final decision to release you from -- from, sorry, Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think the decision came from the president's office in Croatia. A letter arrived, and then information that the military police had provided authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And did you see the letter which gave you -- yes.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never saw the letter. I saw the authorisation form.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Signed by whom?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Perica Juric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please spell the name, full name.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Perica Juric, or Jurkic. He provided the authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What position did he occupy?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think he worked for the police. I don't know what his position was exactly. I didn't really pay much attention to that document. I have it on me [as interpreted], but if you show it to me, I could identify the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 7097.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see the document, Witness?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As you can see, it says: "Release him from Ljubuski." Then it says, "Authorised by Mr. Perica Jukic." Then the person who signed this, the signature says, "The head for the office for exchanges," then it mentions Berislav Pusic, but the authorisation was provided by Perica Jukic. It says on the basis of the guarantees provided, and et cetera, et cetera, release such-and-such a person. I received this document from Tomo Sakota, and I had to show this document at the border in order to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And who provided guarantees to you for your stay in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The guarantee to stay in Zagreb was provided by my aunt's daughter, who lives in Zagreb. And I stayed with her when I studied there. Her name is Muhiba Levan, and she lives in Medvescak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 9578.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the statement given by my relative to the MUP, to the police in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So was it Muhiba Levan --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Levan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Who gave you financial guarantees; yes?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And perhaps I will show you the last document for the Ljubuski. This is Exhibit 4667. If you open the -- in B/C/S version, the page with digits 01520527. That's not the page. 27 should be the last. Page 111. 111, yes. And in English version, it will be page 13. The date, the 10th of December.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see -- could you make out the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can't recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: No. I don't ask that you can recognise or not. Can you read it? Can you understand what is written there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can read it. It's a report on the guard shifts, the brigade police guard shifts in Ljubuski. I can see the date, the 10th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It says, "104 Muslims, two Serbs." That's what it says. It says 12 Serbs and then 12 was crossed out. It says a hospital in Split, one in Livno. It says Muslims 104, two Serbs. It mentions an Albanian and a Catholic. The 10th of 12, 1993, and then it mentions a shift, Dragan Milos, Vinko Radisic, et cetera. Then it says that Radis Santic was released at 9.15 because he was ill and authorisation was obtained from the office for exchange, and Fahrudin Rizvanbegovic was released. He was taken over by Tomo Sakota with the knowledge of the war prison warden, Mato Jelicic. The prisoner was released at 10.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: So is it consistent with what you've just told us about the circumstances of your release from Ljubuski?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Those are the facts that I mentioned a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Mr. Rizvanbegovic, let's pass on to another topic. That's about the destruction in Stolac. When did you see the facts of first instructions -- I'm sorry, destructions have been committed in Stolac during 1990, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993 and 1992, they'd already started setting houses on fire. Mostly Serbian houses were set on fire and blown up. But in 1993, on the 20th of April, 1993, that was on the day that members of the civilian protection were arrested as well as members of the Bregava command, on that day Faruk Pitic's house was set on fire and two days later, a house in Begovina that belonged to Alija Rizvanbegovic was set on fire. This was at done 11.30 on the night between the 22nd and 23rd. Begovina is a cultural monument, and it is a house that is situated within a complex of cultural monuments of the first category.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you see who set on fire Alija Rizvanbegovic's house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see who -- the person or the persons who set it on fire. It was at night. There were two individuals on guard in front of my door. Dragan Peric was one of them, and the other person was Jozo Presic [phoen]. They were standing in front of my door when they shouted out that Alija's house was on fire. We then ran out of the house. We tried to put the fire out. My wife went to a water reservoir was about 3 or 400 metres from our house, and there was a firefighter called Rizovic, and he brought this reservoir, this tank of water, which we used when we attempted to put the fire out from 11.30 until 5.00 in the morning. We weren't able to put the fire out, but we prevented the fire from spreading to the other houses. Unfortunately I do have to say that not a single Croatian soldier wanted to participate in our attempts to put the fire out. Only Muslims, HVO fighters, took part in the attempt to put the fire out. And let me repeat this: I feel very sad when I have to say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Did you report this case to the police?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: On the following morning I immediately went to the civilian police, reported the event to them, described how this had happened. I don't know whether they made a record of any kind, but I didn't sign anything. However, no results were obtained. No member of the police appeared. From the commander of a unit in Begovina -- or to a command of the police was in Begovina, Prce, he was a commander of a platoon in Begovina, and as such it was his duty to inform the military police of the event. I don't know whether he did so or not, but I'm sure that the people from that unit set that house on fire, because no one could reach Begovina without them knowing. They had guards. No one could come from the north of Begovina because the line was above Begovina. The line was to the north. That's where the soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, as has been said, the Judges invite us to abbreviate a little bit the issues, and maybe we should dwell on the cardinal questions relevant to the destruction and other issues which are left here. I am not beating about the bush. I will go straight to Begovina complex. Begovina complex, to what date does the history go back?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The Begovina compound is a historical complex from the end of the 18th century. It belonged to an aristocratic family of Rizvanbegovic. This was the first category cultural monument.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: When was made a decision to declare this complex as a protected complex of first category, or the first category?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: In 1952 by a decision issued by the Bureau for Protection of Cultural Heritage, this decision declared that Begovina was a first category cultural monument, and there was a plaque on the entrance declaring that it was protected by the state. The declaration proclaiming it to be a monument was renewed twice. Every time the law was changed, the decision would be renewed and reissued and placed under the state protection. The last time, I believe, was in 1973 when it was declared to be a listed building. And at that time the decision was expanded not only to the residential buildings but also to other areas including the environment itself, the ambiance. Today, it is listed in the Dayton Accords as a cultural monument that is protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 0001.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see this document?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Could it be enlarged, please? This document is dated 18th of April, 1962, and it refers to a decision issued by the Bureau for Protection of Cultural Sites, under certain number, when this site was declared to be a cultural monument.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Now I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 3842.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: That might not be the best quality, but are you able to make it out?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I have the original, and I'm familiar with this document. I mentioned it a bit ago. It's dated the 31st of July, 1973. I have it in my documentation and also in the documentation of the Bureau for Protection of Cultural Monuments. This decision broadened the protected area. It was broadened not only to include the residential buildings but also the ambiance, the environment around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And for what purposes was your complex, Begovina complex, served?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The Begovina complex consisted of family homes belonging to my family. There were a total of four houses. One belonged to my father, and one belonged to me. In addition, there were four inns. That's what they would be called today. They were dwellings for guests. Then there was also a school, a large number of outbuildings. So there was an entire infrastructure which was typical for aristocratic families of that period. This compound belonged to one of the most prominent, one of the most powerful families of that early period. It included residential buildings, outbuildings, inns for guests, and schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Was it intended for tourist visits?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Just before the war I wanted to open a business there. I made a contract with companies from Dubrovnik, and two or three years before the problems erupted in Croatia, they started bringing visitors. On a yearly basis, several thousand visitors would visit the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Just -- Witness, I would like you to take a look at some pictures and give some explanations so the Trial Chamber could understand or could make some conclusions if really this complex was -- was of great value.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown Exhibit 8918 and with digits 00905254.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you have --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Next page. Digits 00905254. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a portion of the Begovina compound. The house on the left --

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Could you take a marker and show to us, first of all -- electronic marker.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please, Usher, go help the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please encircle it and put number 1, your initials, and date.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Under number 1, the witness encircled the house which belonged to him. And the next building?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The next building belonged to Alija Rizvanbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Please put number 2, again your initials and date.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And under number 2, the witness identified the house belonging to Alija Rizvanbegovic. Is it the house which was burnt down in April?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the house that was put on fire on the 22nd of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Could you move up the picture now, because there is another picture on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what is there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: This is my house nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the registrar -- yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is the house of Alija Rizvanbegovic. This is an identical photograph taken from the same position. The one you saw first was made by me before the war, and I took this picture in 1998. So this is house number 1, and this is house number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... number 3. It's the picture of the house belonging to the witness taken in 1998.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And number 4, the picture taken at the same time, and the house which used to belong to Alija Rizvanbegovic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like this picture to be captured and given e-court numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please give us the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. These are documents marked by the witness. [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... assigned the exhibit number IC 00013. The second picture will be assigned the reference IC 00014. Thank you. Terribly sorry about this. A rectification: The first picture will be assigned IC 00014, the second IC 00015. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to be shown the same exhibit but numbers 00905260. There is something different. Ah, yes. Now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, do you see this picture? What is depicted there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: This is my house from the southern side. You can see the portion of the yard and the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And -- okay. You may put number 5 on this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And also encircle it. Encircle it, this part of the house.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Under number 5, the witness identified the southern side of his house. And now I would like the witness to be shown the same exhibit. Digits number 00905267.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you see, Witness, what --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Not yet. Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Ah, yes. I would like the previous exhibit also be captured and given e-court number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This exhibit will therefore be assigned the reference IC 00016, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, what is depicted here?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a room in my house. This is what it looked like in 1993. This is the interior. The room has carved woodwork, and it had an original screen. Everything was authentic and old. About one and a half century old, almost two centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what value did it represent to history, to architecture, culture?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Since this was a monument of cultural heritage of the first category, then you must know that it is considered to be a very high level document. It was important in the architectural sense and also in terms of its interior. It was perhaps even more important in terms of its interior because it had one of the most beautiful wood carvings. I don't think that there was another example of such beautiful interior in the Balkans. It was rated as the top example of its kind. It was rated so by all of the experts who looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like the witness to take the marker and put number 6 on this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Your signature and date.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: I would like this exhibit to be captured and given an e-court number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: As interior of Mr. Rizvanbegovic's house in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This exhibit will therefore be assigned the reference number IC 00017.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, we know that you were arrested on the 1st of July, 1993. When your complex was destroyed, did you know? When did you know, learn about it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The house of my father was set on fire in the evening, on the 19th of July, 1993, on the day of Saint Alidja, who was then declared to be the patron saint of Stolac. The house was set on fire with the songs glaring over the loudspeakers. My wife was in our neighbour's house and eyewitnessed this. The next day another house was set on fire, and that repeated itself on each of the following days so that the entire Begovina complex was destroyed by this barbarian act. I learned that this had happened once new inmates were brought into Dretelj on the 4th of August, that is to say just several days after this took place. They informed me about this because some of them had stayed on in Stolac after I left. Specifically, I was informed by Esad Sefo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What other buildings in the complex were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: All of the buildings. All of the buildings of this compound were set on fire and burned down to the ground. Only the bathrooms remained in all of the houses, because they were located in the yards, they were not attached to the houses. Deliberately and cynically they left the toilets intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, were there any military storages, other objects, or units deployed, military units deployed in your complex at that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: As I said during my testimony, my brother's house was next to my house. We just shared a wall. In his house a unit was billeted. Several days before my father's house was set afire, that is to say on the 15th, 16th, or 17th of July, this unit left my brother's house and moved into the first house next to Begovina, some 200 metres to the south. It enabled it to control the entire road. Nobody could pass without them noticing. And they went from there to the lines. And it was from this position that they set the houses on fire. The unit was moved away the moment they decided to put the entire -- to set the entire compound on fire. My wife observed this directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And you were talking about some kind of songs that were broadcast at that time. What kind of songs they were singing?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: These songs were known to everyone at the time. They were usually played over the loudspeakers placed on balconies of the houses. Those were Ustasha songs and fascist songs from the Second World War, the songs I mentioned to you earlier in my testimony. This was heard not only by my wife but by everybody in the vicinity. The whole -- the whole street vibrated from these songs. This was like an orgy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: What about mosques in the Stolac area?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: All of the mosques, without exception, were set on fire or blown up. In town itself, four mosques were completely destroyed. Three of them were turned into parking lots, and one of them had just the walls standing. Some 10 kilometres or five kilometres to the south of Capljina and Buna, south of Mostar and Stolac, this was a sort of a triangle, and in that area 22 mosques were either turned into parking lots or blown up. Not a single one was left intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Was your complex, Begovina complex, the only one in Stolac which represented historical and cultural value and protected?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Begovina was just one of the monuments in Stolac. Stolac was a museum. It had dozens of houses which were rated or graded as monuments. One of them was under the protection of the state. The mosques were also protected as cultural monuments. All of the houses which in any way represented the heritage of Islamic and Mediterranean architecture were blown up, destroyed, or set on fire. Not a single one which bore such features was left intact. Your Honours, not a single bullet was fired in Stolac in any combat between the two armies. Not a single bullet. There was absolutely no combat in Stolac. So this entire cultural heritage was destroyed literally by barbarian hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, when did you see -- when did you come back to Stolac for the first time after you had been released?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: For a long time after the federation was founded one couldn't enter Stolac, up until the end of 1997. When the first refugees started going back, I went with my family there. Naturally, I was unable to enter the ruins because everything was covered with weeds. In my kitchen, there was a tree which had grown there, and it was two storeys tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: In what -- in what condition is the Begovina complex now?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Last year we started renewing the Begovina compound owing to the assistance of the Bureau for Protection of Cultural Heritage and also the Ministry of Culture which had initiated this project. We received a donation from the government of Malaysia, so that now we managed to put the roof on one house or, rather, two houses, my house and my brother's house. I hope that this summer we will put the roof on another house and thus protect the walls from further deterioration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Do you live in that complex now?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, I use my own funds to renew the part of the house where I live. My wife is currently there. So I live in Sarajevo for three days in the week while I'm teaching at the university there, and after that I spend the rest of the week in Stolac. And I work tirelessly on repairing the house, and let me tell you, I'm quite fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what about the mosques now? Have they been rebuilt?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The Sara mosque, or the central mosque, has been rebuilt, the one in Moslavici. Alija Rizvanbegovic's mosque is being rebuilt, and I think that the fourth mosque is about to be rebuilt in town. All of the work is conducted by the Bureau for Protection of Cultural Heritage as well as the Islamic community. I'm not very involved in this project so I can't tell you about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Professor, I'd like you to clarify something with regard to the destruction of this complex, because in the indictment, paragraph 166, it says that this paragraph [as interpreted] was allegedly destroyed on the 4th of August, but you said a minute ago that it was on the 19th of July that your brother's house was destroyed, and the destruction continued on the 20th of July. If I've understood you correctly, you found out about this destruction while you were detained and you were detained on the 4th of July. As far as the dates are concerned, what makes you say that it was on the 19th of July? Because in the indictment the date provided is the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for asking me to clarify this. If some misunderstanding occurred, my wife was a witness of this event, and Esad Sefo, who informed me of what happened, was someone she lived with. They were in the immediate vicinity of the complex, and they saw the house being set on fire with their very own eyes. Hundreds of people observed this. It's a large complex. There's a lot of wood there. And when Alija Rizvanbegovic's house was on fire, I must say that the flames lit up the entire town. But on the 4th, I found out that the entire complex had been set on fire. Esad Sefo told me about it. This is the person who came from Stolac. So perhaps a slight error occurred in the indictment, but these are facts that I can confirm. And other witnesses can probably confirm this. My wife is a direct eyewitness of the event and she made a note of the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what your wife said, at the same time as this complex was set on fire were the mosques also set on fire as well as houses in the centre of Stolac? According to what your wife said, did all this -- was all this destruction inflicted on the same day or on the days that followed? What did she tell you exactly because the indictment -- or what is stated in the indictment is not very precise, and as Judges it's necessary for us to describe the exact train of events, so what could you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My wife, since she was my wife, couldn't walk around freely very much, especially since I was detained in a camp. But she said that the town hadn't been set on fire. Once every night certain houses or buildings were set on fire. So this all took place over several days. I think there are sufficient number of witnesses of these events, but because my wife was my wife, it was not advisable for her to walk around the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. The Prosecution may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And my final topic: Witness, did you ever see any group of refugees, Croat refugees, moving around the Stolac area?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion, because to the north of Stolac, in that part mostly -- it's mostly inhabited by Serbs. There aren't any Croats. On one day a large group of Croats, several trucks full of Croats came from the direction of Bileca. We were involved in the Red Cross at the time, so we met them there. There was the late Ale Poljarevic and a certain Boskovic, Andjelko Boskovic, they met them, and we found out that this was a group of Croats from Konjic. They had arrived via Nevesinje to Berkovici. From Berkovici, they carried on as far as Stolac. They were afraid we didn't even know who they were because it was customary for Muslims who had been expelled from Bileca, Gacko, Trebinje, et cetera, to arrive from that direction. We were all surprised to see that these people have arrived -- had arrived from that direction. They were very afraid and it was very difficult for them because I think they had spent two sleepless nights in Nevesinje. That's what they said. And they feared for their lives because some people in that area, some Chetniks, threatened them, called them various names, and they spoke about this very reluctantly, but they did speak about it. And I was a witness of these events when they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And what happened to those people afterwards?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Some of them were taken south of Stolac in the direction of Capljina, and in the southern part of Stolac they were put up in houses. Three settlements were constructed. One was called Suskovo village. The other was called Bobanovo Selo - I assume you know who this concerns - And the third settlement, which was -- the third settlement was south of Stolac in the southern suburbs of Stolac. Some people still live there in these newly constructed settlements. They were built on rocky terrain, and as far as I can now see, not many people live in these settlements today. As far as I can see, only the elderly live there. I think there are very few young people living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Were they all Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of the people living in these settlements were Bosnian Croats. They came from Vares, from Kakanj, there were these people from Konjic, and there were people from other parts of Central Bosnia. They live there now. These settlements were established for them. It was the Republic of Croatia that established these settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: And my final question, and very -- I ask you to answer it very briefly: What is the demographic situation now in Stolac?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN RIZVANBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The Croats returned earlier on, but all the Bosniaks in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and those who had stayed in Germany and other countries in the vicinity returned to Stolac. This return was quite successful. The people loved this town. And I think that the current number is -- well, I think there are slightly more Croats than Bosniaks now, and I can see that this is a situation on the basis of the children in schools. But there are many problems. In the financial part, in the financial office of Stolac, there are only a few Bosniaks. In the administration, there are only a few Bosniaks. The others are Croats. I think there is some sort of apartheid as far as employment is concerned. The Bosniaks can't even invest. They can't launch economic initiatives because you must be aware of the fact that all those who went through the camps were deprived of their possessions, of their money. My wife's money and jewellery was taken. A pupil of hers, since she's a teacher, searched her and searched through her underwear. So everyone from Stolac was robbed. Even people who have certain skills can't launch economic initiatives, can't establish businesses. So this is the problem in Stolac. And the situation is similar as far as poorer Croats are concerned, because the smuggling people were involved in has now ceased. Regardless of the ethnic group they belong to, people are depressed. The situation in the town is very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: Witness, thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PORYVAEV
utterances.text: My examination-in-chief is over. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Tomorrow the hearing will start at 9.00. I will give the floor to the Prosecution so that they can give me a list of all the documents they will be asking to be admitted into evidence. If I have understood this correctly -- but the legal officer will provide me with more precise information. If I've understood this correctly, the Prosecution has taken up four hours. So in accordance with our decision of the 8th of May, our oral decision, the Defence will have eight hours tomorrow. It's for the Defence to see -- I apologise. Four hours. I doubled the amount of time. So Defence counsel will have four hours, and it's for the Defence to decide how to divide this time among themselves. Thank you, and I will see you all tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
